Intronaute — minor-intron retention

168 samples · 734 minor introns · 1528 control introns · hit mode combined · 2026-10-15 09:13
1. Sample map (PCA of minor introns)2. Highest-ranking samples3. Most retained introns4. Shared minor-intron genes5. Build an UpSet plot6. Top events7. Quality control8. Parameters

1. Sample map (PCA of minor introns)

Each point is placed from the continuous score of every measurable minor intron. This report uses z_comb, the same score that has to reach 3 before an intron can be a hit. The map keeps that full value. Introns below the size cutoff in section 4, and introns kept out by the splice-site veto, still move the point. Control introns are left out of this map. A missing score is filled with that intron's cohort median. Extreme values are clipped to -4 through 8 before the axes are fit. Colour by n_hits, and Pin top N, count only the minor introns that pass the hit rule in section 4.
Type in the box to highlight a sample, scroll to zoom, drag to pan, click a point to pin its label. Colour follows the selected score or a samplesheet column. n_hits is how many minor introns are called hits in that sample. tail_q is the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate, across the samples, of the one-sided Fisher test that this sample's minor-intron hit rate is higher than its own control-intron hit rate. A smaller tail_q is stronger evidence. Samples with fewer than 20 measurable introns of either class have no tail_q. Colour by n_hits and Pin top N use the hit count from section 4. The place of each point stays the continuous score above. Colour by −log10(tail_q) stretches a small false-discovery rate so the strongest samples are the high end of the ramp. Samplesheet columns are labels only: they are not used in the scores.
PC1 vs PC2
Each point is one sample, placed from the continuous z_comb of every measurable minor intron. Introns that fail the hit rule in section 4 still move the point. Further right on PC1 means more coordinated retention across minor introns. Further up on PC2 is a second pattern in that profile, often a batch or a different subset of introns.

2. Highest-ranking samples

Switch the table among four rankings. n_hits is how many minor introns are called hits in that sample. n_hits_control is that same hit rule counted on the sample's own U2 control introns. A minor-spliceosome signal raises n_hits above n_hits_control. A noisy library raises both. tail_q is the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate, across the samples, of the one-sided Fisher test that this sample's minor-intron hit rate is higher than its own control-intron hit rate. A smaller tail_q is stronger evidence. Samples with fewer than 20 measurable introns of either class have no tail_q. enrichment is the minor-intron hit rate divided by the control-intron hit rate in that same sample. Each rate is (hits + 0.5) / (measurable introns of that class + 1). Those added counts keep a zero from making the ratio zero or infinite. A value near 1 means minor introns are called about as often as that sample's own control introns. A larger value means the hits are concentrated on minor introns. Samples with fewer than 20 measurable introns of either class have no enrichment. The two plots are the same panels as score_distribution.png. Search highlights a sample on both. Click a dot to pin its name, and click it again to unpin. Colour and pin top N apply to both. Pin top N uses n_hits.

Rank by n_hits
n_hits is how many minor introns are called hits in that sample. Each point is one sample. Rank 1, the leftmost point, has the largest n_hits. The curve falls as that count drops. Search highlights a sample. Click a dot to pin its name.
n_hits vs n_hits_control
n_hits is how many minor introns are called hits in that sample. n_hits_control is that same hit rule counted on the sample's own U2 control introns. A minor-spliceosome signal raises n_hits above n_hits_control. A noisy library raises both. Each point is one sample. The dashed line is equal minor and control hits. Points above the line have n_hits above n_hits_control. Search highlights a sample. Click a dot to pin its name.

3. Most retained introns

Each cell is one minor intron in one sample. The color is that intron's robust z minus the median robust z of the same sample's U2 control introns. When the non-minor introns in that sample are retained too, the cell moves toward white by that amount. Red means this minor intron is retained above the cohort and above that sample's own ordinary introns. Blue means it is below them. The scale is −6 to +6. Every measurable minor intron is shown, labeled by its gene. Slide the figure sideways. The strongest value in these rows is on the left. Switching the ranking changes the samples and can change that order. It does not change the color rule. Hit calls are still the unadjusted z.
n_hits is how many minor introns are called hits in that sample. Each cell is one minor intron in one sample. Red means that intron is retained above the rest of the cohort and above that sample's own control introns. Blue means it is below. Rows are the samples with the largest n_hits. Every measurable minor intron is a column, labeled by its gene. A gene with several minor introns has one column for each. Columns are ordered by the largest adjusted z in these rows, strongest on the left. Slide the figure sideways to see the rest.
n_hits_control is that same hit rule counted on the sample's own U2 control introns. A minor-spliceosome signal raises n_hits above n_hits_control. A noisy library raises both. Rows are the samples with the largest n_hits_control. The columns are again every measurable minor intron, reordered by the largest adjusted z in these rows.
tail_q is the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate, across the samples, of the one-sided Fisher test that this sample's minor-intron hit rate is higher than its own control-intron hit rate. A smaller tail_q is stronger evidence. Samples with fewer than 20 measurable introns of either class have no tail_q. Rows are the samples with the smallest tail_q. A sample can appear here with a smaller n_hits than on the first heatmap when those hits are specific to minor introns. The columns are again every measurable minor intron, reordered by the largest adjusted z in these rows.
−6 below0+6 retained
robust z above this sample's control introns. Blue means this minor intron is below the cohort and below that sample's ordinary introns. Red means it is retained above both. The same scale is on each figure.

4. Shared minor-intron genes

Each person is the set of genes in which a minor intron is a hit and the control introns paired to that minor intron are not. A gene is left out when retention is also called on the matched U2 intron. A blue bar is a combination of people who share those genes. A grey bar is genes found in only one person. The number on a bar is how many genes are in that combination. Bars run from the most genes on the left to the fewest on the right. The table under the plot names the shared genes, in that same order. A group with one person is a list of that person's genes instead of an UpSet plot. The list is labeled with the diagnosis when the sample has one, and with minor spliceopathy otherwise.
Each row of dots is one person. A column is one combination of people. The bar above it is the number of genes with a minor-intron hit, and no hit on the paired control, in exactly those people. Blue combinations are shared by two or more people. Grey combinations are private to one person. Intersection bars run from the most genes on the left to the fewest on the right. The bars on the left are how many genes each person has.

5. Build an UpSet plot

Choose the samples to compare. Each name is labeled with diagnosis and spliceopathy status. minor spliceopathy and a diagnosis button fill the selection. Two or more samples draw an UpSet plot and list every gene combination those people share. Bars run from the most genes on the left to the fewest on the right. One sample lists that person's genes with a minor-intron hit and no hit on the paired control intron. A gene is left out when retention is also called on the matched U2 intron.
Select a group, or pick names below.
Select two or more samples, then Draw. One sample lists that person's genes. Hold Ctrl (or Command) to select several names.

6. Top events

A hit is one intron in one sample. This report uses hit mode combined, and all three checks have to pass. z_comb is at least 3. That score merges how unusual the intron-body coverage is with how unusual the splice sites are, and it is whichever of those two scores is measurable when only one exists. The shift is large on at least one measure: d_cov is at least 0.5, about 1.41 times the cohort-middle intron-to-exon ratio, or d_j is at least 0.5, about 1.41 times the cohort-middle unspliced-to-spliced ratio. When splice-site reads are measurable, z_j is at least 1. A lower splice-site score keeps the intron out of the hit set, because reads in the intron body with ordinary splice sites count as background. When those reads are too few to score, that check is unused and a coverage-driven z_comb can still be a hit. The same rule is applied to minor introns and to U2 control introns.
An event is one minor intron in one sample that passed the hit rule above. Control-intron hits are not listed. The z column is z_comb, the merged score the hit rule tests. The rows are ordered by that score. This table keeps the 60 events with the largest z in the cohort, so one sample can occupy several rows. Per-intron calls are much less reliable than the aggregate score; treat them as candidates to confirm (IGV, then RT-PCR). n_EI_donor and n_EI_acceptor are reads crossing each splice boundary. Retention without them is more likely an overlapping transcript or a mapping artefact.

7. Quality control

A sample with low exonic depth, or with an intronic background far above the rest, should be read with caution. If runs separate here, that is a batch effect, and tail_q is the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate, across the samples, of the one-sided Fisher test that this sample's minor-intron hit rate is higher than its own control-intron hit rate. A smaller tail_q is stronger evidence. Samples with fewer than 20 measurable introns of either class have no tail_q. These are the three panels of qc.png. Colour and search work as on the other plots. n_hits is how many minor introns are called hits in that sample. Pin top N marks the samples with the largest n_hits, so a high-ranking sample can be found on the depth axis.
Median exonic depth
Each point is one sample. This is the typical read depth on the exons used as the denominator of the retention score. A low value means the library may be too shallow for the scores to be trusted.
Fraction of targets measurable
Each point is one sample. This is the share of targets whose flanking exons were deep enough to score. A low value means much of that sample could not be measured.
Intronic background (log2, control introns)
Each point is one sample. This is the control-intron offset subtracted before scoring. A high value means generic intronic background, such as degradation or DNA contamination, rather than U12-specific retention.
Left to right: median exonic depth, the fraction of targets deep enough to score, and the control-intron background. Low depth or a low measurable fraction means the sample is hard to score. A high background means generic intronic noise. When samples are split by run, the bar is that run's median.
n_hits is how many minor introns are called hits in that sample. n_hits_control is that same hit rule counted on the sample's own U2 control introns. A minor-spliceosome signal raises n_hits above n_hits_control. A noisy library raises both. One row is one run. n is how many samples are in that run. n_hits_median and n_hits_max are the median and the maximum n_hits in the run. control_hits_median is the median n_hits_control.
